title: "Abandon all dharmas, come to me alone" (18.66–18.72)
hook: the verse many call the Gita's last word, and the question Krishna asks after it
tomorrow: Sanjaya's closing; "wherever Krishna and Arjuna are" (18.73–18.78)

segments.voice: Yesterday: I have told you, now do as you choose. Reflect fully, then decide, and you are deeply loved. Your line was he hands it back. Today, the verse that comes right after. Day two hundred twenty-five.
screen: `DO AS YOU CHOOSE — HE HANDS IT BACK.`

segments.voice: A child learning to swim. For weeks: kick like this, cup your hands like that, turn your head, breathe. Rules and more rules. Then one day the parent stands in the water, arms open, and says: forget all that. Just come to me. I've got you. The rules weren't wrong. But there's a moment when trust does what technique can't. In one Hindu tradition, the verse right after Krishna hands the choice back is that moment. They call it the charama shloka, the final verse.
screen: `KICK, CUP, TURN, BREATHE.` → `THEN: FORGET ALL THAT.` → `COME TO ME. I'VE GOT YOU.`

segments.voice: Verse sixty-six. Abandoning all dharmas, come to me alone for refuge. I will free you from all wrongs. Do not grieve. Sarva-dharman parityajya, mam ekam sharanam vraja. Commentators have argued over every word. What does abandon all dharmas mean, after a whole book about doing your dharma? Here's who says what. The Sri Vaishnava tradition, which follows Ramanuja, calls this the charama shloka and reads it as surrender, prapatti: stop relying on your own efforts to save yourself, and rely on God's grace alone. Shankara reads it as renouncing all actions and taking refuge in the one self. Other teachers read dharmas here as your anxieties about merit and demerit, not your duties: keep acting, but let go of the scorekeeping. However the first line is read, the verse ends with two words: ma shuchah. Do not grieve. The Gita began with Arjuna grieving, and it ends with Krishna telling him not to. Then verses sixty-seven to seventy-one are about passing the teaching on. Don't tell it to someone who doesn't want to hear it. Whoever shares it with those who love it is most dear. Even someone who only listens to it with faith, without scoffing, finds freedom. And then verse seventy-two. After all that, Krishna asks: Have you heard this with a focused mind, Arjuna? Is your confusion gone? The teacher checks in. That's the last instruction: come for refuge, don't grieve, and did you hear me? That's the word today: abandon all dharmas.
screen: `ABANDON ALL DHARMAS, COME TO ME.` · `THREE READINGS, ONE VERSE.` · `DO NOT GRIEVE.` · `HAVE YOU HEARD THIS, ARJUNA?` · then, large: `ABANDON ALL DHARMAS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and notice what you're carrying today. The rules you're keeping, the scores you're tracking, the ways you're trying to get it all right. Let yourself feel the weight of it. Then, just for these two minutes, set it down. Remember the swimming child, and the open arms in the water. You don't have to believe anything to try this. Just let the weight rest for a moment, and hear the verse's last two words: do not grieve. The bell holds the time.
Abandon all dharmas. Gita eighteen, sixty-six: abandoning all dharmas, come to me alone for refuge; I will free you from all wrongs; do not grieve.
Your line: the last instruction. Today, when you catch yourself keeping score, set it down for one breath, and hear the last two words: do not grieve. Day two hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: In the Sri Vaishnava tradition, Gita 18.66 is honored as the charama shloka, the final verse, and is central to the teaching of surrender (prapatti); teachers in other traditions also give it a central place.

match.prompt: the last verse and its readers — tap the pairs.

myth: all Hindu teachers read 'abandon all dharmas' the same way
the Sri Vaishnava tradition reads surrender; Shankara reads renouncing action for the self; others read letting go of scorekeeping.
the Gita begins with Arjuna grieving and ends with 'do not grieve'
verse 71 says even someone who just listens with faith finds freedom

fork.setup: you're Krishna. you've just given the verse Sri Vaishnavas call the final verse. what do you do next?
options: walk away: the teaching is done.
ask Arjuna whether he heard it and whether his confusion is gone.
fork.reveal: verse 72: have you heard this with a focused mind? is your confusion gone? the teacher checks in.

original.note: Sanskrit: sharanam, refuge, shelter; 'mam ekam sharanam vraja', come to me alone for refuge, Gita 18.66.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'abandon all dharmas' means stop doing your duty.
what it means: readers differ, but the verse turns from rules to refuge, and ends: do not grieve.

what a scholar hears: 18.66 'sarva-dharman parityajya mam ekam sharanam vraja'; the Sri Vaishnava tradition after Ramanuja reads it as prapatti (the charama shloka), Shankara as renouncing all karma for knowledge of the self.

notes: The index word is cut short ('"Abandon all dharmas') because it's the title's head; kept exactly.
Check the three readings of 18.66 (Ramanuja/prapatti; Shankara; 'dharmas' as merit and demerit). The third is attributed only to 'other teachers'.
'Argued over for a thousand years' is approximate (Shankara c. 8th century).

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens 'Think of' or claims 'for many Hindus'; cut 'argued over for a thousand years' (unsourced date), 'every reading agrees' and 'the most human line'; the charama shloka/prapatti reading is now credited to the Sri Vaishnava tradition after Ramanuja rather than to Ramanuja himself (his own bhashya on 18.66 is more varied; the full prapatti reading is developed by later teachers such as Vedanta Desika and Pillai Lokacharya: Keeper to confirm); practice no longer invites the listener to 'be held'; trapdoor's 'most readings say' replaced.
